why.correct: ΔG° = +86.2 kJ/mol > 0: not favored on its own.
options: Counting moles of solid does not decide favorability; ΔG° does, and it is positive.
Right: ΔG° = +86.2 kJ/mol, so the decomposition is not favored.
Many decompositions are not favored (this one, or water into H₂ and O₂).
That would describe kinetic control, which needs ΔG° < 0. Here ΔG° > 0.

why.correct: Adding Reaction 1 and Reaction 2 cancels S(s), the shared intermediate. ΔG° adds: +86.2 + (−300.1) = −213.9 kJ/mol.
Coupling requires a common intermediate. When the steps add, ΔG° values add, and the large negative ΔG° of Reaction 2 carries Reaction 1.
options: Coupling does not change ΔG° of either reaction; the ΔG° values add.
A catalyst cannot make an unfavored reaction favored, and Reaction 2 is not a catalyst.
Reaction 1 has ΔG° = +86.2 kJ/mol whatever else is present; it is the overall reaction that is favored.
Right: a shared intermediate links them, and the sum of ΔG° values is −213.9 kJ/mol.

why.correct: Adding reactions adds ΔG° values and multiplies K values. Check: ΔG° = −213.9 kJ/mol gives K = e^(213,900/2477.6) ≈ 3 × 10³⁷.
options: Right: when reactions add, their K values multiply: (7.8 × 10⁻¹⁶)(4.0 × 10⁵²) ≈ 3 × 10³⁷.
K values do not add when reactions add; they multiply.
Dividing would be for subtracting Reaction 1, not adding it.
ΔG° and K are different quantities, linked by ΔG° = −RT ln K.

why.correct: ΔG°(overall) = ΔG° of Step A + ΔG° of Step B = +13.8 + (−30.5) = −16.7 kJ/mol. The water and phosphate cancel when the steps are added.
An unfavored step is driven by pairing it with a strongly favored one through a common intermediate (here, the phosphate group).
options: Enzymes speed reactions but cannot change ΔG°. The coupling is what makes the overall process favored.
Step A has ΔG° = +13.8 kJ/mol at 37 °C; it is still not favored alone.
Right: the coupled process has ΔG° = −16.7 kJ/mol, so it is favored.
Lowering the product concentration helps a little, but the main driver here is coupling to ATP.

why.correct: ln K = −ΔG°/RT = 16,700 ÷ (8.314 × 310) = 6.48, so K = e^6.48 = 650, about 6.5 × 10². Step A alone has K ≈ 0.0047, so coupling raises K by a factor of about 10⁵.
Coupling works only if ΔG°(driving) + ΔG°(driven) < 0.
options: The sum of ΔG° values must be negative. Here it is positive.
ΔG° values add when reactions are coupled; K values multiply.
Right: the driving reaction must be more favored than the driven one is unfavored.
They need not be equal; the driving reaction just has to outweigh the driven one.

why.correct: Coupling works through a common intermediate that one reaction makes and the other consumes.
options: Right: the shared species links the reactions so they add into one overall process.
Activation energies do not need to match; coupling is about adding reactions.
The ΔG° values usually differ; what matters is that their sum is negative.
Being in the same flask is not enough without a shared species to link them.

why.correct: An unfavored process can be driven by continuously supplying energy from outside, here as electricity. You will see this again in topic 9.8.
options: ΔG° of 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂ is +474.2 kJ/mol whatever drives it; energy has to be supplied.
Lowering a barrier cannot make an unfavored reaction go; energy must be supplied.
Splitting water with a current works at room temperature; the energy comes in as electrical work.
Right: external energy (electric current, light) can drive a process with ΔG° > 0.

why.correct: Photosynthesis is driven by light energy, an external source, coupled through many intermediate steps.
options: Enzymes lower barriers but never change ΔG°.
Right: light is an external energy source, and the plant couples its energy to the unfavored steps.
Making glucose from CO₂ and water has ΔG° far above zero at any leaf temperature.
Removing product changes Q, not ΔG°, and cannot overcome a ΔG° of this size alone.

why.correct: Y is made in reaction 1 and used in reaction 2, so the reactions add to X → Z. ΔG° = +25.0 + (−40.0) = −15.0 kJ/mol.
Coupling does not alter ΔG° of either step. The two steps act as one overall process, and that process has ΔG° = ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂ < 0.
options: Right: each step keeps its own ΔG°; coupling makes the sum negative.
ΔG° values belong to each reaction and simply add; nothing is transferred to change one of them.
The favored reaction stays favored, and the overall process becomes favored if the sum is negative.
Coupling is about adding ΔG° values, not about catalysis.

why.correct: Adding reactions multiplies their K values (and adds their ΔG° values): 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.5 × 10⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁴.
options: K values multiply when reactions add; the smaller K counts too.
Dividing would be for subtracting a reaction, not adding one.
Right: K₃ = K₁ × K₂ = 1.0 × 10⁴, so products are favored.
Adding reactions multiplies K values; it does not divide them.

why.correct: An unfavored process needs a free energy source: a coupled favored reaction or external energy such as electricity or light.
options: The sum of ΔG° values can then be negative.
External electrical work, as when a current splits water, can drive an unfavored process.
A catalyst speeds both directions and cannot make an unfavored process go.
Time helps slow but favored reactions, not unfavored ones.

why.correct: Oxidation happens at the anode. The iron strip loses mass because Fe(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ there.
options: This is the right process for the silver strip, but reduction happens at the cathode, not the anode.
Right: the iron loses mass as Fe atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as ions. Oxidation happens at the anode.
If Fe²⁺ were reduced, the iron strip would gain mass. It loses mass, so iron is oxidized.
If silver were oxidized, the silver strip would lose mass. It gains mass.

why.correct: Oxidation: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. Reduction: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, doubled to use both electrons. Adding gives Fe + 2 Ag⁺ → Fe²⁺ + 2 Ag.
options: Atoms balance but charge does not: +1 on the left, +2 on the right. Each Fe gives two electrons, enough for two Ag⁺.
This is the reverse reaction: it would plate iron and dissolve silver, the opposite of what was observed.
This is a molecular equation; nitrate is a spectator ion and does not appear in the net ionic equation.
Right: two Ag⁺ are reduced for each Fe oxidized, so electrons (2) and charge (+2 on each side) balance.

why.correct: Electrons are released at the anode (iron) and flow through the external wire to the cathode (silver).
options: Right: electrons leave the anode, where iron is oxidized, and travel to the cathode, where Ag⁺ is reduced.
Electrons flow from where they are released (oxidation, iron) to where they are used (reduction, silver).
Electrons travel through the wire; the salt bridge carries ions, not electrons.
Electrons flowing through the wire are the current that the voltmeter detects.

why.correct: Without ion flow, Beaker 1 would build up positive charge (Fe²⁺ made) and Beaker 2 negative charge (Ag⁺ used), and the current would stop.
options: Beaker 1 is gaining positive Fe²⁺ ions, so adding more cations would build up positive charge there.
Each beaker needs one kind of ion to balance its charge: cations to Beaker 2, anions to Beaker 1.
Right: Beaker 2 loses Ag⁺ (a positive charge) and needs cations; Beaker 1 gains Fe²⁺ and needs anions to stay neutral.
A salt bridge carries ions, not electrons, to keep both beakers electrically neutral.

why.correct: The salt bridge completes the circuit by letting ions move. Remove it and the beakers become charged, so electron flow stops.
options: Electrons flow only if ions can move to balance the charge. The circuit is now open.
The two solutions never mix in a working cell; removing the bridge stops the current.
Right: without ion flow the circuit is broken and electrons stop flowing.
There is no closed circuit for any current, in either direction.

why.correct: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): zinc goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized).
options: Right: Zn atoms lose electrons and become Zn²⁺(aq), while Cu²⁺ gains them and plates out.
Cu²⁺ gains electrons to become the copper coating: it is reduced.
Nitrate is a spectator ion here; its oxidation number does not change.
Copper metal is a product in Trial 1, not something that reacts.

why.correct: The cell runs the favored reaction from Trial 3. Copper is oxidized, so the copper electrode is the anode.
options: Trial 4 shows that silver is not oxidized by Cu²⁺; silver ions are reduced instead, at the cathode.
The cost of a metal has nothing to do with which electrode is the anode.
Atomic mass does not decide which metal is oxidized; the observed reaction does.
Right: the favored reaction is Cu + 2 Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2 Ag, so copper is oxidized at the anode.

why.correct: A metal that coats with another metal from solution is being oxidized by those ions. Zn reacts with both ions, Cu with one, Ag with none.
options: This is reversed: silver never reacts, so it is the least easily oxidized.
Right: Zn gives electrons to Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺; Cu gives electrons to Ag⁺ but not to Zn²⁺; Ag gives electrons to neither.
Copper does not react with Zn²⁺ (Trial 2), so zinc is more easily oxidized than copper.
Silver does not react with Cu²⁺ (Trial 4), so copper is more easily oxidized than silver.

why.correct: An electrolytic cell uses an external energy source to drive a thermodynamically unfavored redox reaction.
options: Right: Trial 6 shows Zn²⁺ is not reduced by Ag on its own, so the power supply must drive it.
Plating happens in both kinds of cell. What decides the type is whether the reaction is favored or driven.
In a galvanic cell the reaction itself produces the current; here the current is supplied from outside.
Outside energy can drive an unfavored reaction (topic 9.7); that is what an electrolytic cell does.

why.correct: Reduction always happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode.
options: The anode is where oxidation takes place.
The salt bridge carries ions between half-cells; no redox happens there.
Right: reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode, in both kinds of cell.
The wire carries electrons from the anode to the cathode; it is not where reduction happens.

why.correct: Same definitions of anode and cathode in both; the difference is whether the reaction is favored (galvanic) or driven by outside energy (electrolytic).
options: Oxidation happens at the anode in both kinds of cell.
Right: galvanic cells release free energy as electrical work; electrolytic cells use electrical work.
This is backwards: the electrolytic cell is the one that needs a power supply.
In both, electrons flow through the wire from the anode to the cathode.

why.correct: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode; Sn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Sn at the cathode, so [Sn²⁺] falls.
options: Nickel is the anode (it loses mass), so tin is the cathode.
The salt bridge supplies spectator ions to balance charge; it does not supply Sn²⁺.
Ions do not change identity crossing the bridge, and Ni²⁺ cannot become Sn²⁺.
Right: nickel is oxidized, so tin ions take the electrons and plate out.

why.correct: A galvanic cell separates a favored redox reaction into two half-cells joined by a wire (electrons) and a salt bridge (ions).
options: The oxidation and the reduction must be separated so the electrons go through the wire.
The wire carries electrons from the anode to the cathode.
Ion flow keeps each compartment neutral and completes the circuit.
A galvanic cell needs no power supply; the favored reaction drives the current.
The two half-cells usually contain different metals and ions.
A galvanic cell runs a favored reaction, ΔG° < 0.

why.correct: A cell separates oxidation from reduction so the electrons must flow through the wire. In one beaker they transfer directly and their energy becomes heat.
options: ΔG° does not depend on the container; the reaction is still favored and still happens.
In one beaker the Ag⁺ ions reach the iron directly; that is exactly the problem.
Iron is still oxidized; the difference is only where the electrons go.
Right: separating the half-reactions forces the electrons through the external circuit, where they can do work.

why.correct: Metal from solution coats an electrode by reduction, so the object to be coated is the cathode.
options: Oxidizing the spoon would dissolve steel, not coat it with silver.
Right: the coating forms by reduction, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, which happens at the cathode.
Electrons arrive at the cathode; they leave from the anode.
Plating a metal from its ions is a reduction, which happens at the cathode.

why.correct: At the cathode the species gaining electrons is reduced: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb.
options: This is the oxidation, at the anode.
This would be oxidation of lead, the reverse of what the reaction shows.
Right: lead ions gain electrons (reduction) at the cathode.
Zinc ions are a product here, not a species being reduced.

why.correct: Silver has the more positive E°, so Ag⁺ is reduced (cathode) and Ni is oxidized (anode). E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.80 V − (−0.25 V) = 1.05 V.
Oxidation Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻; reduction 2 Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2 Ag; overall Ni + 2 Ag⁺ → Ni²⁺ + 2 Ag.
options: This is the reverse, with E° = −1.05 V: not favored, so it is not what the galvanic cell runs.
Right: nickel is oxidized, silver ions are reduced, and two Ag⁺ take the two electrons from each Ni.
Atoms balance but charge does not (+1 vs +2). Two electrons need two Ag⁺.
Both metals are oxidized here; a redox reaction needs one species reduced.

why.correct: E°cell is largest when the cathode has the most positive E° and the anode the most negative.
options: E°cell = 0.34 − (−1.66) = 2.00 V, less than the Mg/Ag cell.
E°cell = −0.13 − (−2.37) = 2.24 V, less than with silver as the cathode.
Right: the most positive (+0.80) minus the most negative (−2.37) gives 3.17 V.

why.correct: A reducing agent is oxidized. The metal whose ion has the most negative E° is oxidized most readily.
options: Right: its reduction potential is the most negative, so the reverse, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻, is the most favored oxidation.
Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidizing agent: it is the most easily reduced.
Mg²⁺ is very hard to reduce; it is the weakest oxidizing agent, not a reducing agent.
Silver is the hardest metal in the table to oxidize, so it is the weakest reducing agent.

why.correct: Cu²⁺ has the more positive E°, so it is reduced; Al is oxidized. E°cell = 0.34 V − (−1.66 V) = 2.00 V. The coefficients 2 and 3 used to balance electrons do not change any E°.
n is the least common multiple of the electrons in the two half-reactions: 2 × 3 = 6.
options: That is the electrons for one Al atom. The equation has two Al atoms.
That is the electrons for one Cu²⁺ ion. The equation has three of them.
Right: 2 Al each lose 3 electrons and 3 Cu²⁺ each gain 2: six electrons.
Adding 3 and 2 does not count electrons. Multiply electrons per atom by atoms: 2 × 3 = 3 × 2 = 6.

why.correct: E° is energy per coulomb. Balancing electrons changes the total energy (through n in ΔG° = −nFE°) but not the energy per coulomb.
options: Coefficients do not enter E° at all, whether multiplied or divided.
The coefficients affect n (and so ΔG°), but never E°.
Right: potential is energy per unit charge; doubling the reaction doubles both, leaving E° unchanged.
Neither E° is multiplied.

why.correct: ΔG° = −nFE° and ΔG° = −RT ln K, so E° > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1.
options: Right: a positive cell potential means a favored reaction with products favored at equilibrium.
ΔG° = −nFE°: positive E° gives negative ΔG°.
A negative E°cell gives a positive ΔG° and K < 1.
A negative ΔG° gives K > 1 (ΔG° = −RT ln K).

why.correct: A negative E°cell means ΔG° = −nFE° > 0. The reaction can be driven by a power supply, which is an electrolytic cell.
options: A negative E° means not favored; a catalyst cannot change that.
For this reaction as written, copper would be oxidized; with E° < 0 that does not happen on its own.
At equilibrium the cell potential E is zero, not E°.
Right: a negative E°cell means ΔG° > 0, so the reaction must be driven.

why.correct: ΔG° = −nFE°: doubling the equation doubles n (2 → 4) but not E°, so ΔG° doubles.
options: E° does not double when the equation is doubled.
Right: E° is intensive and stays the same; ΔG° is extensive (n doubles from 2 to 4) and doubles.
Doubling both E° and n would quadruple ΔG°. Neither is right: E° stays 1.10 V.
ΔG° depends on the amount of reaction: twice the equation, twice the free energy.

why.correct: For each reaction, E° = E°(species reduced) − E°(species oxidized). Only the zinc-nickel reaction gives a positive value.
n is the moles of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as written.
options: Right: n counts electrons in the reaction as written, so ΔG° scales with the equation.
This equals n only when each ion gains one electron; n counts electrons, not atoms.
n is a count of electrons transferred, which can be 1, 2, 6 or more.
This equals n only if one anode atom reacts; for 2 Al → 2 Al³⁺, n = 6.

why.correct: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1 only in Trial 1, so only there does E equal E°.
options: The highest voltage comes from Q < 1, not from standard conditions.
Right: standard conditions mean 1 M for every dissolved species, so Q = 1 and E = E° = 1.100 V.
The lowest voltage comes from Q > 1, far from standard conditions.
Standard conditions also require 1 M concentrations, which only Trial 1 has.

why.correct: When Q < 1 the reaction has a larger drive to proceed (ΔG < ΔG°), so E > E°.
options: Electrons in the wire do not depend on the ion concentration. The change in E comes from Q.
E° is fixed (1.10 V); E changes with concentration through Q.
At equilibrium E would be zero. The higher E shows the cell is further from equilibrium.
Right: a lower product concentration (Zn²⁺) or a higher reactant concentration makes Q < 1, raising E above E°.

why.correct: Q > 1 means E < E°. The ratio, not the individual concentrations, decides it.
options: Right: Q = 0.50/0.050 = 10, the same as Trial 4, so E ≈ 1.07 V.
What matters is the ratio Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺], here 10, not whether each is below 1 M.
E equals E° only when Q = 1.
E = 0 only at equilibrium, where Q = K (an enormous number here).

why.correct: As the cell runs, Q rises toward K and E falls toward 0. At equilibrium, Q = K and E = 0.
options: E = E° only at Q = 1; as the cell runs, [Zn²⁺] rises and [Cu²⁺] falls, so Q grows.
Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] grows, not shrinks, as the cell runs.
Right: a "dead" battery is at equilibrium: no net drive, so no voltage.
Left alone, a galvanic cell runs down to equilibrium; it does not overshoot.

why.correct: Both half-cells have the same half-reaction, so E°cell = 0; any voltage measured comes from Q ≠ 1.
options: That is a reduction potential, not a cell potential; subtracting it from itself gives zero.
E°cell is a difference of reduction potentials, never a sum.
Right: E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − 0.34 = 0. The voltage comes only from the concentration difference.
No table is needed: identical half-reactions give E°cell = 0.

why.correct: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(dilute) at the anode, Cu²⁺(concentrated) → Cu(s) at the cathode. Q = [Cu²⁺]dilute/[Cu²⁺]conc = 0.010 < 1, so E > 0.
options: Right: the cell runs to even out the concentrations, so Cu dissolves into the dilute side and Cu²⁺ plates out of the concentrated side.
Making even more Cu²⁺ in the concentrated beaker would widen the difference, raising Q; the cell runs to lower it.
The voltmeter reads a positive voltage, so a net reaction is running.
Each copper strip is an electrode; one is oxidized (anode) and one is reduced (cathode).

why.correct: For a concentration cell K = 1. The cell runs until Q = 1, where E = 0.
options: The total Cu²⁺ does not rise; it moves from one side to the other, shrinking the difference.
E°cell is constant (zero), but E depends on Q, which changes as the cell runs.
The cell stops when the concentrations are equal; it does not overshoot.
Right: as the dilute side gets more concentrated and the concentrated side more dilute, Q → 1 = K and E → 0.

why.correct: Lower Q (further below 1) gives a larger E.
options: The voltage depends on Q, not on how many ions are available.
Right: the larger the concentration difference, the further Q is from 1 and the larger E.
E°cell stays zero, but E depends on Q, which changes.
Dilute solutions still react; a bigger difference gives a bigger voltage.
Right: more products (or fewer reactants) than standard lowers the drive, so E < E°.
That is the case for Q < 1.
That is the case only for Q = 1.
That is the case only at equilibrium, Q = K.

why.correct: E depends on Q = [Ni²⁺]/[Ag⁺]². Raising reactants lowers Q and raises E; raising products does the opposite. Solids and spectator ions do not appear in Q.

variables.name: Adding solid AgNO₃ to the silver half-cell, raising [Ag⁺]
variables.why: More reactant lowers Q, so E rises above E°.

variables.name: Adding solid Ni(NO₃)₂ to the nickel half-cell, raising [Ni²⁺]
variables.why: More product raises Q, so E falls below E°.

variables.name: Using a larger nickel strip of the same metal
variables.why: Solids do not appear in Q, so the size of the strip does not change E.

variables.name: Letting the cell run for an hour
variables.why: As the cell runs, Ag⁺ is used and Ni²⁺ forms, so Q rises and E falls.

variables.name: Replacing the KNO₃ salt bridge with a NaNO₃ salt bridge
variables.why: The salt bridge ions are spectators; they do not appear in Q.

why.correct: A galvanic cell does work until Q = K. Then E = 0 and the cell is "dead".
options: Salt bridge ions can run low, but the basic reason a cell runs down is that Q approaches K.
E° is a fixed property of the half-reactions; it does not change as the cell runs.
Right: there is no longer any net drive, so no current flows, even though reactants may remain.
Electrons come from the oxidation reaction; the cell stops when that reaction reaches equilibrium.

why.correct: ln 1 = 0, so at Q = 1 (standard concentrations) E = E°.
options: ln 0 is not defined; Q = 0 does not make the term zero.
Right: the second term vanishes when ln Q = 0.
At Q = K, E = 0, not E°.
Cells do not run at absolute zero, and E = E° comes from ln Q = 0, not from the temperature.

why.correct: E is largest when Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] is smallest.
options: Q = 100: E falls below E° to about 1.04 V.
Q = 1, so E = E° = 1.10 V: no change.
Solids do not appear in Q, so E is unchanged.
Right: Q = 0.010, the smallest Q of the choices, so E is the largest (about 1.16 V).

why.correct: E° is a fixed standard value; E depends on Q. Q < 1 raises E above E°, Q > 1 lowers it, and E = 0 (not E°) at Q = K.
options: Less product than standard raises the drive.
At equilibrium E = 0; E = E° only at Q = 1.
E° is fixed; E changes.
E is smaller than E° when Q > 1, but it stays positive until Q passes K.

why.correct: E depends on Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. The smaller Q (Cell X) gives the larger E.
options: More product raises Q and lowers E; the number of ions does not set the voltage.
The ratio Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] differs: 0.10 in X, 10 in Y.
E° is the same, but E depends on Q, which differs.
Right: Q(X) = 0.10 and Q(Y) = 10, so E(X) > E° > E(Y).

why.correct: The key gains copper, so Cu²⁺ is reduced on it: the key is the cathode.
options: Gaining electrons is reduction, which happens at the cathode, not the anode.
Right: plating is reduction, which happens at the cathode.
Losing electrons is oxidation, which happens at the anode.
That is what happens at the copper strip, not at the key.

why.correct: 0.2000 mol e⁻ × (1 mol Al / 3 mol e⁻) × 26.98 g/mol = 1.80 g Al.
Same mol e⁻ in each cell; mol metal = mol e⁻ ÷ (electrons per ion), then × molar mass. Silver wins on both counts.
options: A larger charge means more electrons per atom, so fewer atoms form from the same charge.
Equal charge gives equal moles of electrons, but different moles and masses of metal.
There is no balancing; work out each cell: Ag is largest in both moles and mass.
Right: 0.200 mol Ag (21.6 g) versus 0.100 mol Cu (6.36 g) and 0.0667 mol Al (1.80 g).

why.correct: mol metal = mol e⁻ ÷ charge on the ion: 0.200/1 : 0.200/2 : 0.200/3 = 6 : 3 : 2.
options: Right: 0.200 : 0.100 : 0.0667 mol, the ratio 1 : ½ : ⅓, or 6 : 3 : 2.
This follows the charges, but more electrons per ion means fewer moles of metal, not more.
The moles of electrons are equal, not the moles of metal.
Those are the molar masses; the mole ratio depends on electrons per ion.

why.correct: F is the charge of one mole of electrons: 96,485 C/mol e⁻.
options: One electron carries 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; F is that times Avogadro’s number.
F is a charge per mole, not a current, and the metal plated depends on its ion’s charge.
Right: it converts between coulombs and moles of electrons.
F is in coulombs per mole, not volts.

why.correct: The same electrons pass both electrodes. 1 mol e⁻ makes 1 mol Na but only ½ mol Cl₂.
options: Equal electrons, but 1 e⁻ per Na and 2 e⁻ per Cl₂.
Being diatomic means each Cl₂ takes two electrons, so fewer Cl₂ form.
Right: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, and 2 Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
An electrolytic cell drives an unfavored reaction; that is its purpose.

why.correct: Faraday’s law assumes every electron reduces Cu²⁺. Side reactions use some electrons, so less copper forms.
options: Right: if not every electron reduces Cu²⁺, less copper plates than Faraday’s law predicts.
The mass plated depends on the charge, not on the size of the key.
The anode is expected to lose mass as Cu dissolves; it does not reduce the mass plated.
A more concentrated solution would not reduce the copper plated by a given charge.

why.correct: mass = (I t / F) × (1 / electrons per ion) × molar mass. Only the electrons per ion is in the denominator.
options: Doubling the current doubles the charge, which doubles the mass plated.
Doubling the time doubles the charge, which doubles the mass plated.
Same moles, but each mole weighs twice as much: the mass doubles.
Right: twice the electrons per atom means half the moles of metal for the same charge.

why.correct: q = It; mol e⁻ = q/F; mol Cu = mol e⁻ ÷ 2; mass = mol × molar mass.
options: Multiplying by F and by 2 inverts two steps: coulombs ÷ F give mol e⁻, and mol e⁻ ÷ 2 give mol Cu.
Right: charge, then moles of electrons, then moles of metal through the half-reaction, then mass.
Charge is current × time, not current ÷ time.
This skips the 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu step, which doubles the answer.
